messages.body_plain:
Dear Marc,

I have been following this thread and I wish I had found it sooner. I spent countless hours fitting code for Binomial N-Mixture Model and getting weird results. Now I'm aware that I was wrong.

I'm trying to model wolf abundance from an experiment based on camera trap deployment.

We have data from 53 cameras in 770Km ^2 and I have just realised that in our case false positives are facts more than a guess. Also, we account with the misfunctions of some cameras (meaning many 0s and many NAs) So I have my datasets for daily records (90 count units by station), 10 days period records (9 count units by station) and monthly records (3 count units).

So, I would like to adjust the analysis to a Poisson-Poisson, as you suggested here. But, is there any way we could find a source of code where we can start implementing this analysis? I have seen that this example has been left without code in hmecology.

Do you know any reliable paper where this P-P was used and has some guidance on how to code it?

Dear Wenshuang, could you make any progress on this direction?

Thank you very much in advance.

Antonio Sampedro Garrido

> Dear Wenshuang,
>
> the state model of an N-mixture model in algebra looks like this:
>
> N_i ~ Poisson(lambda_i)
>
> N_i is the realized abundance at site i, and lambda_i is the expected abundance at that site. Without a covariate in the model, lambda will be identical for all sites, but N_i will still be different. You can obtain estimates of N_i using function ranef().
>
> To obtain a (perhaps) better characterization of spatial variability in abundance, you could add covariates into the model for lambda, thus doing something like this:
>
> log(lambda_i) = alpha + beta1 * cov1_i + beta2 * cov2_i ....
>
> If these covariates contain information about spatial variation in abundance, then (1) lambda_i will differ among sites and then represent an adequate measure of site-specific abundance, and (2) presumably the estimates of N_i obtained via ranef() will become better still.
>
> Best regards  -- Marc

Dear Antonio,

here is some code for JAGS that I wrote many years ago. Please note also what we wrote in the AHM1 book about this model (Section 6.13.2):

"We believe that this is a very sensible model conceptually, and it can be easily fit in BUGS. Moreover, its parameters can be
estimated with a single visit to each site, i.e., no repeated measurements are required. However, there
may be problems with serial correlation in the detection rate, and in several of our unpublished
applications, the model has not always seemed to produce sensible estimates of abundance. We suggest
that you apply it with caution only ..." ----- "if at all", I am tempted to add here !

This is a high-risk model: while it will work well when its parametric assumptions are perfectly met (as you can convince yourself when analysing simulated data), assumptions are never perfectly met in real life and this is a model which is probably extremely sensitive to assumption violations. On the other hand, more research and more practical explorations for this model are probably a good thing. So why not trying out and reporting back about whether you think results make sense ?

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Marc,

I have been following your wise advice and tried to adjust your Pois-Pois code to the reality of my data. Let me share my steps and my results.

1. My data contains a lot of NAs as cameras were not working simultaneously during the 3 months of experiment. So, some cameras were active since day 1 and others since day 7 or 8 and some of them stopped working after a week or so.

2. Instead of simulating data as you conceived in the code you shared I have changed the variables according to my observations and following your guidance on clustering my records in a single visit. Meaning a matrix with a single column (data$y).
3. lambda = the average unmarked individuals detected by station (1.17)
4. theta = The average number of times that easily recognizable wolves have been detected across all cameras. (9.85) That is how I interpreted the Cue rate, Am I right?
5. T =1
6. I generate the True State with your function and my parameters.
7. I bundle data switching the simulated dataset with my real dataset

(bdata <- list(R = 52, T = 1, y = data$y))

y <- data$y
Nst <- round(apply(y, 1, max)/2)

inits <- function(){list(N = rep(1, data$R), lambda = mean(y)/2, theta = 9.85)}

params <- c("lambda", "theta", "cue.rate", "totalN”)

na <- 1000 ; nc <- 4   ;   ni <- 12000   ;   nb <- 2000   ;   nt <- 1

out <- jags(bdata, inits, params, "NeymanA.txt", parallel = TRUE,
            n.adapt = na, n.chains = nc, n.iter = ni, n.burn = nb, n.thin = nt)

traceplot(out)
print(out, dig = 3)

The result is mysteriously similar to what is expected. In this area, we know 2 packs of wolves and our estimation is about 20-22 wolves in total. Here TotalN= 26.52.

Here is a screenshot of my output.

Does it make sense to you??

If so, I'm ready to start adding Covariates. Thank you very much for your guidance.

Dear Antonio,

thanks for the report. Though your case is of course not a formal test of the model, I nevertheless think that comparisons between estimates and some believed-to-be-known truth in the field can offer some very interesting insight into a model, beyond anything that a simulation study can do.

Couple of comments back:
Yes, the idea is to replace the simulated data with your actual data 🙂 Simulated data just offer a sort of controlled environment within which we can study and understand a statistical model or any other numerical method.
Intuitively, I would NOT aggregate all your data to a single occasion (i.e., T = 1). Though the model can in ideal circumstances be fit with T=1, there is always some loss of information, and I'd just feel better to aggregate the daily raw data perhaps into weekly occasions or some other reasonable duration. Or at the very least I'd do a sensitivity analysis and repeat the procedure for different aggregation schemes and see whether and how much the results change.
Yes, cue rate is exactly theta. Would not really need the two names for the same thing...
It's good to choose inits close to the suspected truth, but I'd also try to run the model without that "initial help" and see whether results still look good (probably they will, but just to check)
I always think we should love but distrust our statistical models. As I said, this model should be particularly distrusted, so you should test it as hard as you can

Thanks again and best regards   --- Marc

messages.subject: Error in AHM2, Sec. 10.5 (binned counts)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

for the AHM project, we don't (currently) have a book website where we can post errors found. Hence, I report an error on this list. This way, there is some chance that users can avoid it.

My colleague Nicolas Strebel just pointed out to me the following error in the data manipulation of the integrated model for binned counts, on page 600 in the AHM2 book. Here, the limits for the dinterval function in JAGS are defined as 0 10 25 50 100 200

However, due to the way how dinterval is defined in JAGS (see page 55 in the manual), this does then not allow a value of 0 for the responses that are in class 1. Therefore, we should have chosen the limits as follows: -1 10 25 50 100 200

In the example in the book, correcting the analysis makes hardly any difference to the inferences, but this will of course not always be so.

Thanks and best regards – Marc

messages.subject: Fitting community occupancy models with spOccupancy
messages.subject_clean: Fitting community occupancy models with spOccupancy
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I just put together some example code that shows how to use R package spOccupancy to fit community occupancy models to an example data set contained in the AHMbook package; happy to share here.

In it, we use a data set with 145 species observed in at least one of 266 1km2 quadrats in the Swiss breeding bird survey MHB in the year 2014. We then use spOccupancy function msPGOcc() to fit two community occupancy models to this data set. The first model is a Null model which for each species just contains an intercept for occupancy and detection, respectively, and where the sets of 145 occupancy and detection parameters are each assumed to be drawn from their own Normal distribution with estimated hyperparameters. The latter represent the community in the model, and the values of the hyperparameters characterize the community in terms of its mean and its species-to-species variance. In the second model we add as species-specific random effects the effects of elevation and forest cover into the occupancy part of the model, and of date and survey duration in the detection part of the model.

These are the very powerful community models discussed in the latter parts of Chapter 11 in the AHM1 book (without data augmentation). spOccupancy now allows us to fit them within 20 minuters rather than 10 hours, as needed when fitting them with JAGS. In addition, we get posterior samples for the z (= species by site presence/absence) matrix. Thus, you could stick the posterior samples of z into any community ecology software such as many functions in package vegan and thereby obtain (1) measures of richness and community composition that are corrected for imperfect detection and (2) a whole posterior distribution for each quantity that vegan gives you.

Finally, if this type of model is important for your work, you might consider our workshop at Sempach in June 2024, where Jeff Doser will cover these models and many more, especially spatial versions of single- and multispecies occupancy and abundance models (http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=8&t=4514&sid=27037d3f81a72ca34270000ce9b2fb75).

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Modeling flight altitudes with a latent parameter
messages.subject_clean: Modeling flight altitudes with a latent parameter
messages.body_plain:
Posting for a colleague -

Hi folks,
I have a model that's trying to fit a gamma distribution to bird altitudes during migration, recorded via GPS transmitters. Our data consists of ~13,000 altitude measurements that are recorded during the day and/or outside of migratory time periods, and so can be safely assumed to be ground locations (true altitude of 0 m). We have another ~ 430 altitude measurements that could potentially be flight locations based on the date and time when they are recorded, but their true movement state is uncertain. Designating this movement state is difficult due to the substantial measurement error in the altitudes (+/- 50 m) and the small number of true flight locations in the sample (believed to be ~33% of recorded nocturnal locations from a prior analysis).

I've built a JAGS model that can infer the measurement error, true movement states, and the distribution of flight locations from the data. In short, it uses the known ground locations to infer the altitudinal measurement error, and then infers unknown states based on the likelihood that a given altitude is solely a result of that measurement error. The measurement error parameters both converge to R-hat values < 1.1 quickly, but the shape and rate parameters take an abnormally large number of iterations (at least 200k) to converge.

After some time working with the simulation, I'm pretty sure that the small sample size of flight locations, combined with the latent variable, are the reasons that the model is taking so long to converge. The model also really doesn't seem to like the gamma distribution; the simulation works much better with a normal distribution, but unfortunately a normal distribution isn't a great fit for the real data.

My questions are:
1) Is the high number of iterations required for convergence a red flag that I shouldn't trust the model output?
2) Is there a way to reparameterize the model so that it samples more effectively? I'm particularly curious about the gamma distribution here. I've also considered moving over to Stan, as it seems to have better mechanisms for dealing with discrete latent variables (i.e. marginalizing them out) but I wanted to rule out a potential JAGS solution first.

I've included a simulation using the model below; note that altitude values (referenced as height above terrain, or HAT, in the code) are scaled with 0 as ground height and 1 being the maximum possible altitude.

Thanks for your time,
Liam Berigan

library(tidyverse)
library(jagsUI)
library(here)

known_ground <- 13000
unknown_flight <- 150
unknown_ground <- 280

# unknown_flight <- 150*50 #model converges with more samples
# unknown_ground <- 280*50

shape <- 1.2470108
rate <- 7.8222304
mean <- shape/rate
sd <- (shape/(rate^2))^.5

measurement_error <- 50/2183.475 #standardized by maximum altitude

known_ground_df <- tibble(HAT = rnorm(n=known_ground, mean=0, sd=measurement_error), HAT_index = rep(1, known_ground))
unknown_ground_df <- tibble(HAT = rnorm(n=unknown_ground, mean=0, sd=measurement_error), HAT_index = rep(NA, unknown_ground))

unknown_flight_df <- tibble(HAT = rgamma(unknown_flight, shape = shape, rate = rate), HAT_index = rep(NA, unknown_flight))
unknown_flight_df$HAT <- map(unknown_flight_df$HAT, function(x){
  rnorm(n=1, mean = x, sd=measurement_error)
}) %>%
  unlist()

dt <- bind_rows(known_ground_df, unknown_ground_df, unknown_flight_df)

sink(here("simulation_gamma.jags"))
cat("model{
   # likelihood
    for (i in 1:n_obs){
    HAT[i] ~ dnorm(mu_observed[i], tau_error) # adding gps-specific error
    mu_observed[i] <- mu_bias + (HAT_index[i]-1)*real_alt[i] # on average, the observed altitude should be the real altitude + the average bias
    real_alt[i] ~ dgamma(shape_flight, rate_flight) # distribution of real flight altitudes
    }

    #priors
    for (k in 1:n_obs){
    HAT_index[k] ~ dcat(c(0.67, 0.33)) # 1 is a ground location, 2 is a flight location.
    }

    mu_bias ~ dnorm(0, 1) #negative values allowed
    tau_error <- pow(sigma_error, -2) #precision
    sigma_error ~ dnorm(0, 1) T(0,) #standard deviation

    shape_flight ~ dnorm(0, prec_shape) T(0,)
    prec_shape <- pow(5, -2)
    rate_flight ~ dnorm(0, prec_rate) T(0,)
    prec_rate <- pow(10, -2)

}
    ")
sink()

inits <- function(){list(mu_bias = rnorm(1,0,1),
                         sigma_error = runif(1,0,1),
                         shape_flight = runif(1,0,5), #
                         rate_flight = runif(1,0,10))}

parameters <- c("mu_bias", "sigma_error", "shape_flight", "rate_flight") #

jags_data <- list(HAT = dt$HAT,
                  n_obs = nrow(dt),
                  HAT_index = dt$HAT_index)
# running jags
nc <- 3 # number of chains
ni <- 5000 # number of iterations
nb <- 2000 # burnin
nt <- 1 # thin rate (keeps every 5th iteration)
m_test <- jags(data=jags_data, inits=inits, parameters.to.save = parameters,
               model.file=here("simulation_gamma.jags"), n.chains=nc, n.iter=ni, n.burnin=nb,
               parallel=T)

print(m_test)

traceplot(m_test)

--

messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I am struggling to solve an error that is probably related to the dmnorm.vcov() function in JAGS.

My response variable is the logit version of occupancy probability as it was estimated by an occupancy model. From the occupancy model I extracted 100 posterior samples for 217 species for each of 4 land types. I now want to see whether the response depends on species functional traits mass (logarithmized and standardized) and their trophic.niche (categorical with 7 levels) while correcting for their phylogenetic relatedness (variable phylo.effect).
A colleague helped me to set up the following model which worked for him and his dataset, but I cannot solve the error with my data.

# LIKELIHOOD
  for(k in 1:nspecies){         # loop over species
    for(i in 1:npost){          # loop over posterior samples extracted from multi-species occupancy model
      for(h in 1:nland.types){  # loop over land types
        psi.logit[i,h,k] ~ dnorm(mu[i,h,k], tav.res)
        mu[i,h,k] <- alpha0 + alpha1[h]*mass.l.st <http://mass.l.st>[k] + alpha2[h,trophic.niche[k]] + phylo.effect[k]
      } } }

  # phylogenetic effect
  phylo.effect[1:nspecies] ~ dmnorm.vcov(rep(0,nspecies), sd.species^2*phylo.cov[1:nspecies,1:nspecies])

  for(k in 1:nspecies){
    for(s in 1:nspecies){
      phylo.cov[k,s] <- exp(delta0*phylo.dist.s[k,s])   # generates species covariance matrix
    }}

  # PRIORS
  # linear-model parameters
  alpha0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  for(h in 1:nland.types){
    alpha1[h] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    for(t in 1:ntrophic.niches){
      alpha2[h,t] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    }}

  # phylogenetic components
  delta0 ~ dunif(-100, 0)            # phylogenetic signal
  sd.species ~ dt(0, 1, 1)T(0,)

  # residual variance (= sd.res^2)
  sd.res ~ dt(0, 1, 1)T(0,)
  tav.res <- 1/sd.res^2

The resulting error is:
Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) : 2 nodes produced errors; first error: Error in node phylo.effect Invalid parent values
I obtain this error independent of whether I provide initial values or not and whether I allow the model to estimate delta0 and sd.species or I define them deterministically, e.g., delta0=-1 and sd.species=0.1. I guess the error occurs, because JAGS is not happy with the parameters I provide in brackets behind dmnorm.vcov(), but I don't see what is wrong with them: a vector of zeros for the mean should be okay, and the covariance matrix is a realistic (and positive) covariance matrix multiplied by a positive variance.

Does anyone spot where I made a mistake or know how to solve this problem?
R-code and data are attached.
In case this is of any importance, I am using R version 4.3.2 and jagsUI version 1.5.2.

Thank you in advance!

Gesa

Update on my previously posted problem:

Combining suggestions on- and off-list by Matthijs Hollanders and Thomas Riecke, I could resolve the error by doing 2 things:
I restructured the model to use dmnorm(rep(0,nspecies), Omega[1:nspecies, 1:nspecies]) instead of dmnorm.vcov() on the covariance matrix itself, see new model code below.
I also added a diagonal matrix of tiny values (0.001) to the covariance matrix (now called Sigma) to ensure that it is positive definite before I take its inverse Omega = precision matrix (see attached code). The non-positive definite covariance matrix was actually what created the error. And why it was not positive definite to start with, I still need to figure out...
Big thanks to Matthijs and Thomas for your quick and excellent help!!! ✨

Gesa

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Updated model code (changes in red, full revised code and data attached):

  # LIKELIHOOD
  for(k in 1:nspecies){         # loop over species
    for(i in 1:npost){          # loop over posterior samples extracted from multi-species occupancy model
      for(h in 1:nland.types){  # loop over land types
        psi.logit[i,h,k] ~ dnorm(mu[i,h,k], tav.res)
        mu[i,h,k] <- alpha0 + alpha1[h]*mass.l.st <http://mass.l.st>[k] + alpha2[h,trophic.niche[k]] + phylo.effect[k]
      }}}

  # phylogenetic effect

  phylo.effect[1:nspecies] ~ dmnorm(rep(0,nspecies), Omega[,])
  Omega[1:nspecies, 1:nspecies] <- inverse(Sigma[,]) * tav.phy

  # PRIORS
  # linear-model parameters
  alpha0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  for(h in 1:nland.types){
    alpha1[h] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    for(t in 1:ntrophic.niches){
      alpha2[h,t] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    }}

  # phylogenetic components

  sd.phy ~ dunif(0, 2)
  tav.phy <- 1/sd.phy^2

  # residual variance (= sd.res^2)
  sd.res ~ dt(0, 1, 1)T(0,)
  tav.res <- 1/sd.res^2

messages.subject: MCMC algorithm for CJS model
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I have been trying to write my own MCMC algorithm in R for an CJS model, but encountered some issues. My code is adapted from the Hooten and Hefley book: while they only considered a model with constant survival and capture probabilities, I want to make it work for a model with temporally varying survival and capture probabilities as functions of separate covariates. Also, I'm hoping to make the model work with data in the individual encounter history format (I did get the model work after converting the data into an m-array). My algorithm seems to provide biased estimates for a few parameters, while the bias seems to be related to shrinkage of survival probabilities to the mean (see attached figures). I wonder if this is just the property of the model, or I did anything wrong in the algorithm. In any case, it will be greatly appreciated if someone can either point me to a code source which I can learn from or look at my code (attached) and see if there is any mistake in it. Thank you.

PS: If you want to run my code, you could use the attached covariate data, which will allow you to get the same results as mine (since a seed is used).

Best regards,
Qing

messages.subject_clean: predict() using stPGOcc model in spOccupancy
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to use the model results from an stPGOcc analysis (through the spOccupancy package in R) to predict responses for detection and occurrence in a broader landscape.

I had a few questions regarding the build of the X.0 object directly from the data object used in the original model.

The data object of the original model contains the data matrix 'y', 'occ.covs', 'det.covs', and the coords. In the case of missing data, the data object can be used in the stPGOcc model after removing NA rows in the 'y' data matrix. This is the model procedure I've followed - by subsetting the 'data' object to generate a 'data_NAremoved' object (or list of lists) to run the analysis. I would now like to predict occurrence and detection from the model on all sites contained in the original 'data' object.

I wanted to know if it would be possible to subset the 'data' object in a manner that allows for the generation of the X.0 design matrix directly, rather than building the X.0 matrix from scratch. The considerations would be to scale the covariates properly, based on the mean and sd values of the scaled covariates used in the original model, and only 'predict' on the new sites, or to 'predict' using the full dataset (effectively a double prediction for the sites used in the creation of the model).

I'm having trouble with the creation of X.0 from scratch, and was not able to properly follow using the example code found in https://rdrr.io/github/doserjef/spOccupancy/man/predict.stPGOcc.html
